author: WorldBriefDaily
text:
Spain has confirmed a second hantavirus case linked to the deadly MV Hondius cruise ship outbreak. Both patients are now in quarantine in Madrid, along with 12 other close contacts under medical observation. The new case was detected through routine PCR screening.

Unlike typical hantavirus, the Andes strain involved can transmit between people via prolonged close contact. This is why authorities have placed all exposed individuals in a 42-day military hospital quarantine.The WHO issued an international alert but maintains low risk to the general public. So far, Spain’s containment has been effective—no community spread detected. However, with 3 deaths among the 8–11 cases on the ship, the situation remains serious for those quarantined.

Source: Euronews; WHO

author: HantaTracking
text:
All 27 passengers and crew aboard the MV Hondius who remained under observation in the Netherlands have now tested negative for hantavirus, according to Dutch health officials.

The article says the testing was conducted after the deadly outbreak linked to the Andes strain of hantavirus triggered international monitoring and quarantine efforts across multiple countries.

Dutch authorities said no new infections were identified among the group, while investigations and follow-up monitoring continue for other exposed travelers internationally.

The report also notes that the ship recently arrived in Rotterdam for cleaning and disinfection procedures following the outbreak.

author: Global_Arab_Net
text:
France and the Netherlands have announced that all individuals who had contact with patients infected with the Hantavirus linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius have tested negative for the disease.

In France, 26 people who were under observation after contact with infected passengers have been cleared following negative test results. Similarly, Dutch authorities confirmed that all passengers who arrived on evacuation flights from the ship this week tested negative.

The ship was the subject of an international health alert regarding the rare virus, which is typically transmitted by rodents. While some passengers remain in medical isolation as a precaution, health officials have emphasized that the risk to the general public remains low. One American passenger who initially received an inconclusive positive test result has also since tested negative. Globally, there have been three deaths and six confirmed cases associated with this outbreak.

#Hantavirus #HealthUpdate #PublicHealth #GlobalArabNetwork

author: YahooNews
text:
Seventeen people under observation in Italy and Spain for possible hantavirus infection have tested negative, the countries' health ministries said on Wednesday as governments around the globe track the virus to ‌stop it from spreading.

The MV Hondius cruise ship, which had confirmed hantavirus cases on board, is expected to arrive at the ‌Dutch port of Rotterdam on Monday, shipowner Oceanwide Expeditions said, adding that the remaining 25 crew members, along with two medical staff, will follow quarantine procedures set by Dutch ​authorities upon arrival.

The World Health Organization said on Tuesday more cases were expected from the cluster that broke out on the ship during a polar expedition that departed from Argentina, but it stressed this was nothing like COVID and was not a pandemic. https://t.co/MGbKVX1brK

🚨 🛳️🦠 CRUISE VIRUS CLUSTER — MARKETS WATCH FEAR, NOT PANIC

Health officials are monitoring a hantavirus cluster linked to the MV Hondius cruise ship, with reported cases, deaths and exposed U.S. passengers placed under observation after repatriation.

This is where the story needs balance. Authorities say wider public risk remains low, but markets remember how travel fear can hit confidence fast when headlines spread.

The pressure point is travel and cruise sentiment. Clear containment can limit damage. More confirmed cases can weigh on cruise stocks, airlines and risk mood.

author: CBSMornings
text:
A more than 40-day observation period is underway for 18 Americans who were aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship, connected to several deadly cases of the Andes strain of the hantavirus. Most of those Americans, including one who tested positive for the virus, are at a quarantine center in Nebraska.

Public health officials are continuing to remind the public that this is not the beginning of another pandemic: “It didn't make sense to have a, sort of, five-alarm fire bell."
